report:
The current best evidence does not support that saw palmetto improves BPH symptoms long-term compared with placebo — the opposite of your stated view.

**What the strongest evidence shows:**

- **NEJM 2006 trial (Bent et al.)**: A rigorous year-long, double-blind, placebo-controlled RCT in men with moderate-to-severe BPH found saw palmetto was **not superior to placebo** for AUA symptom scores, urinary flow, prostate size, or quality of life (https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa053085).

- **CAMUS trial**: Even tripling the standard dose (up to 960 mg/day) over 72 weeks showed **no benefit over placebo**; the placebo group scored marginally better, and no dose-response effect was found (https://urologyandmenshealth.com/saw-palmetto-bph-evidence-review/).

- **Updated Cochrane systematic review** (the highest-quality synthesis, pooling multiple RCTs): Concluded that **Serenoa repens (saw palmetto) monotherapy does not improve LUTS or peak urinary flow compared with placebo**, even at double or triple the usual dose, and that evidence for combination phytotherapy products remains uncertain (https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD001423_serenoa-repens-benign-prostatic-hyperplasia).

- **NCCIH (NIH) summary**: Echoes this conclusion — while early small studies suggested modest benefit, larger, better-designed trials and the Cochrane review found saw palmetto **no more effective than placebo** for BPH urinary symptoms (https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/providers/digest/spotlight-on-saw-palmetto-science).

**Caveats:** Some smaller/earlier trials and certain proprietary extracts (e.g., Permixon) reported modest benefits, and product standardization varies widely across studies, which may explain inconsistent findings. But the largest, longest, most rigorous trials and systematic reviews converge on a negative result.

**Conclusion:** Based on the best available evidence, saw palmetto does **not** reliably improve BPH symptoms over placebo in the longer term.
